The **United States secretary of education** is the head of the [United States Department of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Education "United States Department of Education"). The secretary serves as the principal advisor to the president of the United States, and the federal government, on policies, programs, and activities related to all education in the United States. As a member of the [Cabinet of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_United_States "Cabinet of the United States"), the secretary is sixteenth in the [line of succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_line_of_succession "United States presidential line of succession") to the [presidency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education#cite_note-2) Prior to its creation as an Executive Department, there was a non-Cabinet level position called the [United States commissioner of education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Commissioner_of_Education "United States Commissioner of Education") who led the [United States Office of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Office_of_Education "United States Office of Education").

The current secretary of education is [Linda McMahon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linda_McMahon "Linda McMahon"), serving in this role under President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education#cite_note-3)

## Function

The United States secretary of education is a member of the [president's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") [Cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_United_States "Cabinet of the United States") and is the sixteenth in the [United States presidential line of succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_line_of_succession "United States presidential line of succession").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education#cite_note-4) This secretary deals with federal influence over [education policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Education_policy "Education policy"), and heads the United States Department of Education.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education#cite_note-5)

The secretary is advised by the [National Advisory Committee on Institutional Quality and Integrity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NACIQI "NACIQI"), an advisory committee, on "matters related to accreditation and to the eligibility and certification process for institutions of higher education."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education#cite_note-6)

## List of secretaries

Prior to the creation of the Department of Education in 1979, Education was a division of the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare.

# At a Glance: U.S. Secretaries of Education

The U.S. Department of Education has had 13 secretaries since its birth as a Cabinet-level department in 1980. Some have served for an entire presidential administration, others for less than a year. They’ve used their perch at the helm of the Education Department to push a broad basket of policy priorities, from standardized testing and broader civil rights enforcement to a rollback of the federal footprint in K-12. And they’ve come from a range of backgrounds, including that of former governor, federal judiciary, state schools chief, big-city superintendent, and outspoken policy advocate.

Check out these pages for a deep look at each secretary’s tenure, challenges, and accomplishments.

# U.S. Department of Education

News and analysis right to your inbox. [Click](https://ballotpedia.org/Ballotpedia_Email_Updates "Ballotpedia Email Updates") to get Ballotpedia’s newsletters!

From Ballotpedia

Jump to: [navigation](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#mw-navigation), [search](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#p-search)

See also: *[United States education agencies](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_education_agencies "United States education agencies")*

The **U.S. Department of Education** is a United States executive department established in 1980. The department was formed to promote educational excellence and ensure equal opportunity for public schooling.[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-DOEabout-1) Of the 15 Cabinet agencies, the U.S. Department of Education has the smallest staff and the third largest discretionary budget.[[2]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-2)  

[Linda McMahon](https://ballotpedia.org/Linda_McMahon "Linda McMahon") is the U.S. secretary of education. [Click here](https://ballotpedia.org/Confirmation_process_for_Donald_Trump%27s_Cabinet_nominees,_2025-2026 "Confirmation process for Donald Trump's Cabinet nominees, 2025-2026") to learn more about her confirmation process.

## History

Education in the U.S. is primarily the responsibility of states and local districts. The [United States Constitution](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_Constitution "United States Constitution") does not mention any role for the federal government in education, and, according to the [Tenth Amendment](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_Constitution "United States Constitution"), anything not mentioned in the [Constitution](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_Constitution "United States Constitution") is left to the states to decide. A federal department of education was originally created in 1867 to help the states set up school systems by gathering information about teaching, schools, and teachers. The current U.S. Department of Education was established by [Congress](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_Congress "United States Congress") in 1980. It united several existing offices across different agencies into a Cabinet level agency located in the executive branch. Over the years, the location of the department in the government and its name has changed several times, and its scope, number of personnel and budget has significantly increased.[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-DOEabout-1)[[3]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-3)

The department's mission of fostering educational excellence and equal access arose out of the cultural and political events in the post-World War II era. The [National Defense Education Act (NDEA)](https://ballotpedia.org/National_Defense_Education_Act_(NDEA) "National Defense Education Act (NDEA)"), the first comprehensive federal education law, was passed by Congress in 1958 in response to the Soviet launch of Sputnik during the Cold War. The department added its "public access" mission in response to anti-poverty and civil rights legislation of the 1960s and 1970s.[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-DOEabout-1)[[4]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-4)

Although the federal government provides only about 12 percent of the overall education spending of $1.15 trillion, the role of the federal government in setting education policy has grown considerably over the last several decades. The department implements laws passed by Congress and administers grants to states for certain programs, such as the [No Child Left Behind Act](https://ballotpedia.org/No_Child_Left_Behind_Act "No Child Left Behind Act"), [Race to the Top](https://ballotpedia.org/Race_to_the_Top "Race to the Top") and Title One School Improvement Grants.[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-DOEabout-1)[[5]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-6)

### Timeline

The following is a list of important dates in the history of the federal government's role in education:[[7]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-hist-7)[[8]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-8)

- 1862: The First Morrill Act provided the first federal aid for higher education by donating land for setting up colleges.[[9]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-9)
- 1890: The Second Morrill Act established a support system for land-grant colleges and universities.
- 1896: The [U.S. Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Supreme Court of the United States") case *[Plessy v. Ferguson](https://ballotpedia.org/Plessy_v._Ferguson "Plessy v. Ferguson")* legalized segregation in "separate but equal" schools.
- 1917: The Smith-Hughes Act extended federal aid to vocational education programs.
- 1944: The GI Bill authorized assistance to veterans for postsecondary schools.
- 1946: The Georgia-Barden Act established agricultural, industrial and home economics classes.
- 1954: The U.S. Supreme Court case *[Brown v. Board of Education](https://ballotpedia.org/Brown_v._Board_of_Education "Brown v. Board of Education")* outlawed segregation precedent set in *Plessy v. Ferguson*.
- 1958: The [National Defense Education Act (NDEA)](https://ballotpedia.org/National_Defense_Education_Act_(NDEA) "National Defense Education Act (NDEA)") supported loans for college students; improved science, technology and foreign language support in elementary and secondary schools; and provided fellowships in response to the Cold War.
- 1964: Title VI of the [Civil Rights Act](https://ballotpedia.org/Civil_Rights_Act_of_1964 "Civil Rights Act of 1964") prohibited discrimination based on race, color or national origin in public schools.
- 1965: Title I of the [Elementary and Secondary Education Act](https://ballotpedia.org/Elementary_and_Secondary_Education_Act_of_1965 "Elementary and Secondary Education Act of 1965") gave federal aid to schools in poor rural and urban areas.
- 1965: The Higher Education Act authorized federal aid for poor postsecondary students.
- 1970: Standardized tests were given to public schools and the results were reported to the government and public in an effort to hold educators accountable.
- 1972: Title IX of the Education Amendments prohibited discrimination based on sex in public schools.
- 1973: Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act prohibited discrimination based on disability in public schools.
- 1980: Congress passed the "Department of Education Organization Act," (Public Law 96-88 of October 1979).
- 2001: The [No Child Left Behind Act](https://ballotpedia.org/No_Child_Left_Behind_Act "No Child Left Behind Act") (NCLB) increased education funding and established standards-based testing reforms.
- 2010: The [Race to the Top](https://ballotpedia.org/Race_to_the_Top "Race to the Top") program encouraged states to compete for federal grants in education.
- 2025: Education Secretary [Linda McMahon](https://ballotpedia.org/Linda_McMahon "Linda McMahon") announced the U.S. Department of Education would transfer the administration of some federal K-12 and higher education programs to the [U.S. Department of Labor](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Labor "U.S. Department of Labor"), the [U.S. Department of the Interior](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_the_Interior "U.S. Department of the Interior"), the [U.S. Department of Health and Human Services](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services "U.S. Department of Health and Human Services"), and the [U.S. Department of State](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_State "U.S. Department of State").[[10]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-10)

## Mission

The U.S. Department of Education's official department mission statement is as follows:

- “ ED's mission is to promote student achievement and preparation for global competitiveness by fostering educational excellence and ensuring equal access. Congress established the U.S. Department of Education (ED) on May 4, 1980, in the Department of Education Organization Act (Public Law 96-88 of October 1979). Under this law, ED's mission is to:

- Strengthen the Federal commitment to assuring access to equal educational opportunity for every individual;

- Supplement and complement the efforts of states, the local school systems and other instrumentalities of the states, the private sector, public and private nonprofit educational research institutions, community-based organizations, parents, and students to improve the quality of education;

- Encourage the increased involvement of the public, parents, and students in Federal education programs;

- Promote improvements in the quality and usefulness of education through Federally supported research, evaluation, and sharing of information;

- Improve the coordination of Federal education programs;

- Improve the management of Federal education activities; and

- Increase the accountability of Federal education programs to the President, the Congress, and the public.[[11]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-quotedisclaimer-11) ”
- —Department of Education[[12]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-mission-12)

## [Noteworthy events](https://ballotpedia.org/Noteworthy_events "Noteworthy events")

#### U.S. Department of Education enters into agreements to transfer administration of some education programs to four federal agencies (2025)

On November 18, Education Secretary [Linda McMahon](https://ballotpedia.org/Linda_McMahon "Linda McMahon") announced the [U.S. Department of Labor](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Labor "U.S. Department of Labor"), the [U.S. Department of the Interior](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_the_Interior "U.S. Department of the Interior"), the [U.S. Department of Health and Human Services](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services "U.S. Department of Health and Human Services"), and the [U.S. Department of State](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_State "U.S. Department of State") would administer some federal K-12 and higher education programs through six interagency agreements with the U.S. Department of Education.[[13]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-press-13)[[14]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-14)

McMahon said the partnerships supported President [Donald Trump's](https://ballotpedia.org/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") March 20, 2025, [executive order](https://ballotpedia.org/Executive_Order:_Improving_Education_Outcomes_by_Empowering_Parents,_States,_and_Communities_(Donald_Trump,_2025) "Executive Order: Improving Education Outcomes by Empowering Parents, States, and Communities (Donald Trump, 2025)") that called for closing the Education Department and returning its functions to the states.[[15]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-15) McMahon said, "The Trump Administration is taking bold action to break up the federal education bureaucracy and return education to the states. Cutting through layers of red tape in Washington is one essential piece of our final mission."[[13]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-press-13)

McMahon announced the following partnerships:[[13]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-press-13)

- **U.S. Department of Labor**: Elementary and Secondary Education Partnership
- **U.S. Department of Labor**: Postsecondary Education Partnership
- **U.S. Department of the Interior**: Indian Education Partnership
- **U.S. Department of Health and Human Services**: Foreign Medical Accreditation Partnership
- **U.S. Department of Health and Human Services**: Child Care Access Means Parents in School Partnership
- **U.S. Department of State**: International Education and Foreign Language Studies Partnership

#### Supreme Court allows President Trump's order to dismantle DOE to continue pending litigation (2025)

The [U.S. Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Supreme_Court "U.S. Supreme Court") allowed the Trump administration to resume enforcement of a March 20 executive order to shut down the Department of Education (DOE), pending the administration's appeal of a May 22, 2025, ruling by U.S. District Judge [Myong Joun](https://ballotpedia.org/Myong_Joun "Myong Joun") that blocked it. The May ruling also ordered the administration to reinstate fired workers. In a lawsuit, several education groups claimed that the Trump executive order hindered the department's ability to fulfill its mandated responsibilities, which include providing financial aid, supporting special education, and protecting civil rights. The executive order, titled "Improving Education Outcomes by Empowering Parents, States, and Communities," was written to shift education authority to the states and close the DOE beyond its "core necessities" of distributing Title I funding for low-income schools, money for special education, and Pell grants. On March 11, 2025, the Trump Administration laid off 1,300 workers, leaving the department with half its former workforce and most significantly impacting Federal Student Aid, the Office for Civil Rights, and the [Institute of Education Sciences](https://ballotpedia.org/Institute_of_Education_Sciences "Institute of Education Sciences"). Joun wrote that the layoffs "will likely cripple the Department," and noted that "the Department cannot be shut down without Congress’s approval." The Trump administration filed an appeal days later. The [U.S. Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Supreme_Court "U.S. Supreme Court") allowed the Trump administrative to resume enforcement of the executive order, pending the appeal.[[16]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-18)

#### Trump administration rescinds Obama-era guidance document (2018)

*See also: [Guidance (administrative state)](https://ballotpedia.org/Guidance_(administrative_state) "Guidance (administrative state)") and [Rulemaking](https://ballotpedia.org/Rulemaking "Rulemaking")*

The Trump administration rescinded [guidance](https://ballotpedia.org/Guidance "Guidance") documents in July 2018 that had been issued by the DOE under the Obama administration. The [guidance](https://ballotpedia.org/Guidance "Guidance") documents encouraged institutions of higher education to consider race as a factor in the admissions process as a means to achieving student diversity. The documents provided legal recommendations and contextual examples for schools considering race as a component of the admissions process.[[19]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-cnn-19)[[20]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-wsj-20)

The decision to rescind the DOE's [guidance](https://ballotpedia.org/Guidance "Guidance") documents occurred in light of an investigation launched by the [U.S. Department of Justice](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Justice "U.S. Department of Justice") (DOJ) in the summer of 2017 regarding allegations that Harvard University discriminated against Asian-American applicants by holding them to a higher standard than other applicants.[[20]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-wsj-20)[[21]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-21)

Attorney General [Jeff Sessions](https://ballotpedia.org/Jeff_Sessions "Jeff Sessions") announced the policy change on July 3, 2018. In his announcement, Sessions stated that the DOE is required to adopt new regulations through the [rulemaking](https://ballotpedia.org/Rulemaking "Rulemaking") process, which provides members of the public with the opportunity to offer feedback on [proposed rules](https://ballotpedia.org/Proposed_rule "Proposed rule") during [public comment periods](https://ballotpedia.org/Comment_period "Comment period"). He discouraged the agency from implementing regulations through [guidance](https://ballotpedia.org/Guidance "Guidance") documents, which are issued by agencies in order to explain, interpret, or advise interested parties about rules, laws, and procedures:[[19]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-cnn-19)

| “ | The American people deserve to have their voices heard and a government that is accountable to them. When issuing regulations, federal agencies must abide by constitutional principles and follow the rules set forth by Congress and the President. In previous administrations, however, agencies often tried to impose new rules on the American people without any public notice or comment period, simply by sending a letter or posting a guidance document on a website. That's wrong, and it's not good government.[[19]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-cnn-19)[[11]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-quotedisclaimer-11) | ” |
| --- | --- | --- |

Sessions previously instructed the DOJ to refrain from issuing regulations through [guidance](https://ballotpedia.org/Guidance "Guidance") documents in a November 2017 agency memo. For more information about Sessions' DOJ memo on [guidance](https://ballotpedia.org/Guidance "Guidance"), [**click here**](https://ballotpedia.org/Guidance_(administrative_state)#Presidential_administrations_on_guidance "Guidance (administrative state)").

## Secretaries of foreign affairs (1781–1789)

On January 10, 1780, the [Congress of the Confederation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congress_of_the_Confederation "Congress of the Confederation") created the Department of Foreign Affairs.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_secretaries_of_state#cite_note-1)

On August 10, 1781, Congress selected [Robert R. Livingston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_R._Livingston "Robert R. Livingston"), a delegate from [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)"), as the first secretary for foreign affairs. Livingston was unable to take office until October 20, 1781. He served until June 4, 1783, and was succeeded by [Elias Boudinot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elias_Boudinot "Elias Boudinot"), who was succeeded by [John Jay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Jay "John Jay") on December 21, 1784, who served until March 4, 1789, when the government under the [Articles of Confederation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Articles_of_Confederation "Articles of Confederation") gave way to the government under the [Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_the_United_States "Constitution of the United States").

The office of secretary of foreign affairs and the Department of Foreign Affairs were reinstated by a law signed by [George Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington "George Washington") on July 27, 1789. [John Jay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Jay "John Jay") retained the post on an interim basis, pending the return of [Thomas Jefferson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson "Thomas Jefferson") from France.

## Secretaries of state

On September 15, 1789, before Jefferson could return to take the post, Washington signed into law another act which changed the name of the office from Secretary of Foreign Affairs to [Secretary of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_State "United States Secretary of State"), changed the name of the department to the [Department of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_State "United States Department of State"), and added several domestic powers and responsibilities to both the office of secretary and the department. [Thomas Jefferson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson "Thomas Jefferson") took office as the first secretary of state on March 22, 1790.

This is a list of United States secretaries of state by time in office. This is based on the difference between dates; if counted by number of calendar days all the figures would be one greater. [Cordell Hull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordell_Hull "Cordell Hull") is the only person to have served as secretary of state for more than eight years. [Daniel Webster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Webster "Daniel Webster") and [James G. Blaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_G._Blaine "James G. Blaine") are the only secretaries of state to have ever served non-consecutive terms. [Warren Christopher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Christopher "Warren Christopher") served very briefly as acting secretary of state non-consecutively with his later tenure as full-fledged secretary of state. [Elihu B. Washburne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elihu_B._Washburne "Elihu B. Washburne") served as secretary of state for less than two weeks before becoming [ambassador to France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ambassadors_of_the_United_States_to_France "List of ambassadors of the United States to France").

The **United States secretary of education** is the head of the [United States Department of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Education "United States Department of Education"). The secretary serves as the principal advisor to the president of the United States, and the federal government, on policies, programs, and activities related to all education in the United States. As a member of the [Cabinet of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_United_States "Cabinet of the United States"), the secretary is sixteenth in the [line of succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_line_of_succession "United States presidential line of succession") to the [presidency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education#cite_note-2) Prior to its creation as an Executive Department, there was a non-Cabinet level position called the [United States commissioner of education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Commissioner_of_Education "United States Commissioner of Education") who led the [United States Office of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Office_of_Education "United States Office of Education").

The current secretary of education is [Linda McMahon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linda_McMahon "Linda McMahon"), serving in this role under President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education#cite_note-3)

## Function

The United States secretary of education is a member of the [president's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") [Cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_United_States "Cabinet of the United States") and is the sixteenth in the [United States presidential line of succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_line_of_succession "United States presidential line of succession").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education#cite_note-4) This secretary deals with federal influence over [education policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Education_policy "Education policy"), and heads the United States Department of Education.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education#cite_note-5)

The secretary is advised by the [National Advisory Committee on Institutional Quality and Integrity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NACIQI "NACIQI"), an advisory committee, on "matters related to accreditation and to the eligibility and certification process for institutions of higher education."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education#cite_note-6)

## List of secretaries

Prior to the creation of the Department of Education in 1979, Education was a division of the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare.

# At a Glance: U.S. Secretaries of Education

The U.S. Department of Education has had 13 secretaries since its birth as a Cabinet-level department in 1980. Some have served for an entire presidential administration, others for less than a year. They’ve used their perch at the helm of the Education Department to push a broad basket of policy priorities, from standardized testing and broader civil rights enforcement to a rollback of the federal footprint in K-12. And they’ve come from a range of backgrounds, including that of former governor, federal judiciary, state schools chief, big-city superintendent, and outspoken policy advocate.

Check out these pages for a deep look at each secretary’s tenure, challenges, and accomplishments.

# U.S. Department of Education

News and analysis right to your inbox. [Click](https://ballotpedia.org/Ballotpedia_Email_Updates "Ballotpedia Email Updates") to get Ballotpedia’s newsletters!

From Ballotpedia

Jump to: [navigation](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#mw-navigation), [search](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#p-search)

See also: *[United States education agencies](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_education_agencies "United States education agencies")*

The **U.S. Department of Education** is a United States executive department established in 1980. The department was formed to promote educational excellence and ensure equal opportunity for public schooling.[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-DOEabout-1) Of the 15 Cabinet agencies, the U.S. Department of Education has the smallest staff and the third largest discretionary budget.[[2]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-2)  

[Linda McMahon](https://ballotpedia.org/Linda_McMahon "Linda McMahon") is the U.S. secretary of education. [Click here](https://ballotpedia.org/Confirmation_process_for_Donald_Trump%27s_Cabinet_nominees,_2025-2026 "Confirmation process for Donald Trump's Cabinet nominees, 2025-2026") to learn more about her confirmation process.

## History

Education in the U.S. is primarily the responsibility of states and local districts. The [United States Constitution](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_Constitution "United States Constitution") does not mention any role for the federal government in education, and, according to the [Tenth Amendment](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_Constitution "United States Constitution"), anything not mentioned in the [Constitution](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_Constitution "United States Constitution") is left to the states to decide. A federal department of education was originally created in 1867 to help the states set up school systems by gathering information about teaching, schools, and teachers. The current U.S. Department of Education was established by [Congress](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_Congress "United States Congress") in 1980. It united several existing offices across different agencies into a Cabinet level agency located in the executive branch. Over the years, the location of the department in the government and its name has changed several times, and its scope, number of personnel and budget has significantly increased.[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-DOEabout-1)[[3]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-3)

The department's mission of fostering educational excellence and equal access arose out of the cultural and political events in the post-World War II era. The [National Defense Education Act (NDEA)](https://ballotpedia.org/National_Defense_Education_Act_(NDEA) "National Defense Education Act (NDEA)"), the first comprehensive federal education law, was passed by Congress in 1958 in response to the Soviet launch of Sputnik during the Cold War. The department added its "public access" mission in response to anti-poverty and civil rights legislation of the 1960s and 1970s.[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-DOEabout-1)[[4]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-4)

Although the federal government provides only about 12 percent of the overall education spending of $1.15 trillion, the role of the federal government in setting education policy has grown considerably over the last several decades. The department implements laws passed by Congress and administers grants to states for certain programs, such as the [No Child Left Behind Act](https://ballotpedia.org/No_Child_Left_Behind_Act "No Child Left Behind Act"), [Race to the Top](https://ballotpedia.org/Race_to_the_Top "Race to the Top") and Title One School Improvement Grants.[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-DOEabout-1)[[5]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-6)

### Timeline

The following is a list of important dates in the history of the federal government's role in education:[[7]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-hist-7)[[8]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-8)

- 1862: The First Morrill Act provided the first federal aid for higher education by donating land for setting up colleges.[[9]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-9)
- 1890: The Second Morrill Act established a support system for land-grant colleges and universities.
- 1896: The [U.S. Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Supreme Court of the United States") case *[Plessy v. Ferguson](https://ballotpedia.org/Plessy_v._Ferguson "Plessy v. Ferguson")* legalized segregation in "separate but equal" schools.
- 1917: The Smith-Hughes Act extended federal aid to vocational education programs.
- 1944: The GI Bill authorized assistance to veterans for postsecondary schools.
- 1946: The Georgia-Barden Act established agricultural, industrial and home economics classes.
- 1954: The U.S. Supreme Court case *[Brown v. Board of Education](https://ballotpedia.org/Brown_v._Board_of_Education "Brown v. Board of Education")* outlawed segregation precedent set in *Plessy v. Ferguson*.
- 1958: The [National Defense Education Act (NDEA)](https://ballotpedia.org/National_Defense_Education_Act_(NDEA) "National Defense Education Act (NDEA)") supported loans for college students; improved science, technology and foreign language support in elementary and secondary schools; and provided fellowships in response to the Cold War.
- 1964: Title VI of the [Civil Rights Act](https://ballotpedia.org/Civil_Rights_Act_of_1964 "Civil Rights Act of 1964") prohibited discrimination based on race, color or national origin in public schools.
- 1965: Title I of the [Elementary and Secondary Education Act](https://ballotpedia.org/Elementary_and_Secondary_Education_Act_of_1965 "Elementary and Secondary Education Act of 1965") gave federal aid to schools in poor rural and urban areas.
- 1965: The Higher Education Act authorized federal aid for poor postsecondary students.
- 1970: Standardized tests were given to public schools and the results were reported to the government and public in an effort to hold educators accountable.
- 1972: Title IX of the Education Amendments prohibited discrimination based on sex in public schools.
- 1973: Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act prohibited discrimination based on disability in public schools.
- 1980: Congress passed the "Department of Education Organization Act," (Public Law 96-88 of October 1979).
- 2001: The [No Child Left Behind Act](https://ballotpedia.org/No_Child_Left_Behind_Act "No Child Left Behind Act") (NCLB) increased education funding and established standards-based testing reforms.
- 2010: The [Race to the Top](https://ballotpedia.org/Race_to_the_Top "Race to the Top") program encouraged states to compete for federal grants in education.
- 2025: Education Secretary [Linda McMahon](https://ballotpedia.org/Linda_McMahon "Linda McMahon") announced the U.S. Department of Education would transfer the administration of some federal K-12 and higher education programs to the [U.S. Department of Labor](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Labor "U.S. Department of Labor"), the [U.S. Department of the Interior](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_the_Interior "U.S. Department of the Interior"), the [U.S. Department of Health and Human Services](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services "U.S. Department of Health and Human Services"), and the [U.S. Department of State](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_State "U.S. Department of State").[[10]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-10)

## Mission

The U.S. Department of Education's official department mission statement is as follows:

- “ ED's mission is to promote student achievement and preparation for global competitiveness by fostering educational excellence and ensuring equal access. Congress established the U.S. Department of Education (ED) on May 4, 1980, in the Department of Education Organization Act (Public Law 96-88 of October 1979). Under this law, ED's mission is to:

- Strengthen the Federal commitment to assuring access to equal educational opportunity for every individual;

- Supplement and complement the efforts of states, the local school systems and other instrumentalities of the states, the private sector, public and private nonprofit educational research institutions, community-based organizations, parents, and students to improve the quality of education;

- Encourage the increased involvement of the public, parents, and students in Federal education programs;

- Promote improvements in the quality and usefulness of education through Federally supported research, evaluation, and sharing of information;

- Improve the coordination of Federal education programs;

- Improve the management of Federal education activities; and

- Increase the accountability of Federal education programs to the President, the Congress, and the public.[[11]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-quotedisclaimer-11) ”
- —Department of Education[[12]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-mission-12)

## [Noteworthy events](https://ballotpedia.org/Noteworthy_events "Noteworthy events")

#### U.S. Department of Education enters into agreements to transfer administration of some education programs to four federal agencies (2025)

On November 18, Education Secretary [Linda McMahon](https://ballotpedia.org/Linda_McMahon "Linda McMahon") announced the [U.S. Department of Labor](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Labor "U.S. Department of Labor"), the [U.S. Department of the Interior](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_the_Interior "U.S. Department of the Interior"), the [U.S. Department of Health and Human Services](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services "U.S. Department of Health and Human Services"), and the [U.S. Department of State](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_State "U.S. Department of State") would administer some federal K-12 and higher education programs through six interagency agreements with the U.S. Department of Education.[[13]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-press-13)[[14]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-14)

McMahon said the partnerships supported President [Donald Trump's](https://ballotpedia.org/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") March 20, 2025, [executive order](https://ballotpedia.org/Executive_Order:_Improving_Education_Outcomes_by_Empowering_Parents,_States,_and_Communities_(Donald_Trump,_2025) "Executive Order: Improving Education Outcomes by Empowering Parents, States, and Communities (Donald Trump, 2025)") that called for closing the Education Department and returning its functions to the states.[[15]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-15) McMahon said, "The Trump Administration is taking bold action to break up the federal education bureaucracy and return education to the states. Cutting through layers of red tape in Washington is one essential piece of our final mission."[[13]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-press-13)

McMahon announced the following partnerships:[[13]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-press-13)

- **U.S. Department of Labor**: Elementary and Secondary Education Partnership
- **U.S. Department of Labor**: Postsecondary Education Partnership
- **U.S. Department of the Interior**: Indian Education Partnership
- **U.S. Department of Health and Human Services**: Foreign Medical Accreditation Partnership
- **U.S. Department of Health and Human Services**: Child Care Access Means Parents in School Partnership
- **U.S. Department of State**: International Education and Foreign Language Studies Partnership

#### Supreme Court allows President Trump's order to dismantle DOE to continue pending litigation (2025)

The [U.S. Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Supreme_Court "U.S. Supreme Court") allowed the Trump administration to resume enforcement of a March 20 executive order to shut down the Department of Education (DOE), pending the administration's appeal of a May 22, 2025, ruling by U.S. District Judge [Myong Joun](https://ballotpedia.org/Myong_Joun "Myong Joun") that blocked it. The May ruling also ordered the administration to reinstate fired workers. In a lawsuit, several education groups claimed that the Trump executive order hindered the department's ability to fulfill its mandated responsibilities, which include providing financial aid, supporting special education, and protecting civil rights. The executive order, titled "Improving Education Outcomes by Empowering Parents, States, and Communities," was written to shift education authority to the states and close the DOE beyond its "core necessities" of distributing Title I funding for low-income schools, money for special education, and Pell grants. On March 11, 2025, the Trump Administration laid off 1,300 workers, leaving the department with half its former workforce and most significantly impacting Federal Student Aid, the Office for Civil Rights, and the [Institute of Education Sciences](https://ballotpedia.org/Institute_of_Education_Sciences "Institute of Education Sciences"). Joun wrote that the layoffs "will likely cripple the Department," and noted that "the Department cannot be shut down without Congress’s approval." The Trump administration filed an appeal days later. The [U.S. Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Supreme_Court "U.S. Supreme Court") allowed the Trump administrative to resume enforcement of the executive order, pending the appeal.[[16]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-18)

#### Trump administration rescinds Obama-era guidance document (2018)

*See also: [Guidance (administrative state)](https://ballotpedia.org/Guidance_(administrative_state) "Guidance (administrative state)") and [Rulemaking](https://ballotpedia.org/Rulemaking "Rulemaking")*

The Trump administration rescinded [guidance](https://ballotpedia.org/Guidance "Guidance") documents in July 2018 that had been issued by the DOE under the Obama administration. The [guidance](https://ballotpedia.org/Guidance "Guidance") documents encouraged institutions of higher education to consider race as a factor in the admissions process as a means to achieving student diversity. The documents provided legal recommendations and contextual examples for schools considering race as a component of the admissions process.[[19]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-cnn-19)[[20]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-wsj-20)

The decision to rescind the DOE's [guidance](https://ballotpedia.org/Guidance "Guidance") documents occurred in light of an investigation launched by the [U.S. Department of Justice](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Justice "U.S. Department of Justice") (DOJ) in the summer of 2017 regarding allegations that Harvard University discriminated against Asian-American applicants by holding them to a higher standard than other applicants.[[20]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-wsj-20)[[21]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-21)

Attorney General [Jeff Sessions](https://ballotpedia.org/Jeff_Sessions "Jeff Sessions") announced the policy change on July 3, 2018. In his announcement, Sessions stated that the DOE is required to adopt new regulations through the [rulemaking](https://ballotpedia.org/Rulemaking "Rulemaking") process, which provides members of the public with the opportunity to offer feedback on [proposed rules](https://ballotpedia.org/Proposed_rule "Proposed rule") during [public comment periods](https://ballotpedia.org/Comment_period "Comment period"). He discouraged the agency from implementing regulations through [guidance](https://ballotpedia.org/Guidance "Guidance") documents, which are issued by agencies in order to explain, interpret, or advise interested parties about rules, laws, and procedures:[[19]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-cnn-19)

| “ | The American people deserve to have their voices heard and a government that is accountable to them. When issuing regulations, federal agencies must abide by constitutional principles and follow the rules set forth by Congress and the President. In previous administrations, however, agencies often tried to impose new rules on the American people without any public notice or comment period, simply by sending a letter or posting a guidance document on a website. That's wrong, and it's not good government.[[19]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-cnn-19)[[11]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-quotedisclaimer-11) | ” |
| --- | --- | --- |

Sessions previously instructed the DOJ to refrain from issuing regulations through [guidance](https://ballotpedia.org/Guidance "Guidance") documents in a November 2017 agency memo. For more information about Sessions' DOJ memo on [guidance](https://ballotpedia.org/Guidance "Guidance"), [**click here**](https://ballotpedia.org/Guidance_(administrative_state)#Presidential_administrations_on_guidance "Guidance (administrative state)").

The **United States secretary of education** is the head of the [United States Department of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Education "United States Department of Education"). The secretary serves as the principal advisor to the president of the United States, and the federal government, on policies, programs, and activities related to all education in the United States. As a member of the [Cabinet of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_United_States "Cabinet of the United States"), the secretary is sixteenth in the [line of succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_line_of_succession "United States presidential line of succession") to the [presidency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education#cite_note-2) Prior to its creation as an Executive Department, there was a non-Cabinet level position called the [United States commissioner of education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Commissioner_of_Education "United States Commissioner of Education") who led the [United States Office of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Office_of_Education "United States Office of Education").

The current secretary of education is [Linda McMahon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linda_McMahon "Linda McMahon"), serving in this role under President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education#cite_note-3)

## Function

The United States secretary of education is a member of the [president's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") [Cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_United_States "Cabinet of the United States") and is the sixteenth in the [United States presidential line of succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_line_of_succession "United States presidential line of succession").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education#cite_note-4) This secretary deals with federal influence over [education policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Education_policy "Education policy"), and heads the United States Department of Education.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education#cite_note-5)

The secretary is advised by the [National Advisory Committee on Institutional Quality and Integrity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NACIQI "NACIQI"), an advisory committee, on "matters related to accreditation and to the eligibility and certification process for institutions of higher education."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education#cite_note-6)

*The Commerce Secretary's office as it looked in the mid-20th century.*

The **United States secretary of commerce** (**SecCom**) is the head of the [United States Department of Commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Commerce "United States Department of Commerce"). The secretary serves as the principal advisor to the [president of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") on all matters relating to [commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commerce "Commerce"). The secretary reports directly to the president and is a statutory member of the [Cabinet of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_United_States "Cabinet of the United States"). The secretary is [appointed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prerogative "Prerogative") by the president, with the [advice and consent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advice_and_Consent_Clause "Advice and Consent Clause") of the [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate"). The secretary of commerce is responsible for promoting American businesses and industries. The department states its mission as 'to foster, promote, and develop the foreign and domestic commerce of the United States'.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Commerce#cite_note-2)

Until 1913, there was one [secretary of commerce and labor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Commerce_and_Labor "United States Department of Commerce and Labor"), uniting this department with the [United States Department of Labor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Labor "United States Department of Labor"), which is now headed by a separate [United States secretary of labor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Labor "United States Secretary of Labor").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Commerce#cite_note-3)

The secretary of commerce is a [Level I position in the Executive Schedule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_Schedule#Level_I "Executive Schedule")[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Commerce#cite_note-4) with an annual salary of [US$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Dollar "US Dollar") 250,600, as of January 2025.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Commerce#cite_note-Salary-5)

The current secretary of commerce is [Howard Lutnick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_Lutnick "Howard Lutnick").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Commerce#cite_note-6)

5. [Under Secretary of Commerce for Standards and Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Under_Secretary_of_Commerce_for_Standards_and_Technology "Under Secretary of Commerce for Standards and Technology")
6. [Under Secretary of Commerce for Oceans and Atmosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Under_Secretary_of_Commerce_for_Oceans_and_Atmosphere "Under Secretary of Commerce for Oceans and Atmosphere") and Administrator of the [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Oceanic_and_Atmospheric_Administration "National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration")
7. Under Secretary of Commerce for Export Administration

# Secretaries of State - Principal Officers - People - Department History

Congress created the position of Secretary of State on Jul 27, 1789 (1 Stat.
 28), as the principal officer of the Department of Foreign Affairs (later renamed
 Department of State). The Secretary was to perform such duties as the President
 required, in accordance with the Constitution, relating to correspondence,
 commission, or instructions to U.S. ministers or consuls abroad, and to conduct
 negotiations with foreign representatives.

The Secretary has also served as principal adviser to the President in the
 determination and execution of U.S. foreign policy and in recent decades has become
 responsible for overall direction, coordination, and supervision of
 interdepartmental activities of the U.S. Government overseas, except for certain
 military activities.

The Act of Congress of Sep 5, 1789, that changed the name of the Department of
 Foreign Affairs assigned various domestic duties to the Department of State. Nearly
 all were later reassigned to other agencies. This list does not include individuals
 designated to act as Secretaries of State when the Secretaryship was vacant. These
 individuals are usually referred to collectively as Secretaries of State ad
 interim.

# Secretaries of State - Principal Officers - People - Department History

Congress created the position of Secretary of State on Jul 27, 1789 (1 Stat.
 28), as the principal officer of the Department of Foreign Affairs (later renamed
 Department of State). The Secretary was to perform such duties as the President
 required, in accordance with the Constitution, relating to correspondence,
 commission, or instructions to U.S. ministers or consuls abroad, and to conduct
 negotiations with foreign representatives.

The Secretary has also served as principal adviser to the President in the
 determination and execution of U.S. foreign policy and in recent decades has become
 responsible for overall direction, coordination, and supervision of
 interdepartmental activities of the U.S. Government overseas, except for certain
 military activities.

The Act of Congress of Sep 5, 1789, that changed the name of the Department of
 Foreign Affairs assigned various domestic duties to the Department of State. Nearly
 all were later reassigned to other agencies. This list does not include individuals
 designated to act as Secretaries of State when the Secretaryship was vacant. These

This is a **list of secretaries of state of the United States**.

## Secretaries of foreign affairs (1781–1789)

On January 10, 1780, the [Congress of the Confederation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congress_of_the_Confederation "Congress of the Confederation") created the Department of Foreign Affairs.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_secretaries_of_state#cite_note-1)

On August 10, 1781, Congress selected [Robert R. Livingston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_R._Livingston "Robert R. Livingston"), a delegate from [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)"), as the first secretary for foreign affairs. Livingston was unable to take office until October 20, 1781. He served until June 4, 1783, and was succeeded by [Elias Boudinot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elias_Boudinot "Elias Boudinot"), who was succeeded by [John Jay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Jay "John Jay") on December 21, 1784, who served until March 4, 1789, when the government under the [Articles of Confederation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Articles_of_Confederation "Articles of Confederation") gave way to the government under the [Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_the_United_States "Constitution of the United States").

The office of secretary of foreign affairs and the Department of Foreign Affairs were reinstated by a law signed by [George Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington "George Washington") on July 27, 1789. [John Jay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Jay "John Jay") retained the post on an interim basis, pending the return of [Thomas Jefferson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson "Thomas Jefferson") from France.

## Secretaries of state

On September 15, 1789, before Jefferson could return to take the post, Washington signed into law another act which changed the name of the office from Secretary of Foreign Affairs to [Secretary of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_State "United States Secretary of State"), changed the name of the department to the [Department of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_State "United States Department of State"), and added several domestic powers and responsibilities to both the office of secretary and the department. [Thomas Jefferson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson "Thomas Jefferson") took office as the first secretary of state on March 22, 1790.

This is a list of United States secretaries of state by time in office. This is based on the difference between dates; if counted by number of calendar days all the figures would be one greater. [Cordell Hull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordell_Hull "Cordell Hull") is the only person to have served as secretary of state for more than eight years. [Daniel Webster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Webster "Daniel Webster") and [James G. Blaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_G._Blaine "James G. Blaine") are the only secretaries of state to have ever served non-consecutive terms. [Warren Christopher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Christopher "Warren Christopher") served very briefly as acting secretary of state non-consecutively with his later tenure as full-fledged secretary of state. [Elihu B. Washburne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elihu_B._Washburne "Elihu B. Washburne") served as secretary of state for less than two weeks before becoming [ambassador to France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ambassadors_of_the_United_States_to_France "List of ambassadors of the United States to France").

The **United States secretary of health and human services** is the head of the [United States Department of Health and Human Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Department of Health and Human Services"), and serves as the principal advisor to the [president of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") on health matters. The secretary is a member of the [United States Cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Cabinet "United States Cabinet"). [Robert F. Kennedy Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_F._Kennedy_Jr. "Robert F. Kennedy Jr.") is the incumbent secretary of health and human services, having held the position since February 13, 2025.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_Secretaries_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-2)

The office was formerly known as the secretary of health, education, and welfare. In 1980, the [Department of Health, Education, and Welfare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Health,_Education,_and_Welfare "United States Department of Health, Education, and Welfare") was renamed to Department of Health and Human Services, and its education functions and [Rehabilitation Services Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rehabilitation_Services_Administration "Rehabilitation Services Administration") were transferred to the new [United States Department of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Education "United States Department of Education").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_Secretaries_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-3) [Patricia Roberts Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patricia_Roberts_Harris "Patricia Roberts Harris") headed the department before and after it was renamed.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_Secretaries_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-4)

Nominations to the office are referred to the [Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Health,_Education,_Labor,_and_Pensions "United States Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions") and the [United States Senate Committee on Finance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Finance "United States Senate Committee on Finance"), which has jurisdiction over Medicare and Medicaid,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_Secretaries_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-5) before confirmation is considered by the full [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate"). The secretary of health and human services is a [level I position in the Executive Schedule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_Schedule#Level_I "Executive Schedule"),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_Secretaries_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-6) thus earning a salary of [US$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Dollar "US Dollar")250,600, as of January 2025.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_Secretaries_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-Salary-7)

## Duties

[![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/28/Flag_of_the_Secretary_of_Health%2C_Education%2C_and_Welfare.png/250px-Flag_of_the_Secretary_of_Health%2C_Education%2C_and_Welfare.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Flag_of_the_Secretary_of_Health,_Education,_and_Welfare.png)

*The flag of the secretary of health, education, and welfare, the predecessor to the current office*

The duties of the secretary revolve around human conditions and concerns in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"). This includes advising the [president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") on matters of [health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health "Health"), [welfare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_security "Social security"), and income security programs. The secretary strives to administer the Department of Health and Human Services to carry out approved programs and make the public aware of the objectives of the department.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_Secretaries_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-8)

The [Department of Health, Education and Welfare](https://simple.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Health,_Education,_and_Welfare "simple:United States Department of Health, Education, and Welfare") (HEW) was reorganized into a [Department of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Education "United States Department of Education") and a [Department of Health and Human Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Department of Health and Human Services") (HHS).

The Department of Health and Human Services oversees 11 agencies including the [Food and Drug Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Food_and_Drug_Administration "Food and Drug Administration") (FDA), [Centers for Disease Control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Disease_Control "Centers for Disease Control") (CDC), [National Institutes of Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Institutes_of_Health "National Institutes of Health") (NIH), [Administration for Children and Families](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administration_for_Children_and_Families "Administration for Children and Families") (ACF) and [Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Medicare_and_Medicaid_Services "Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services") (CMS).[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_Secretaries_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-9)

## Line of succession

The line of succession for the secretary of health and human services is as follows:[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_Secretaries_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-11)

1. [Deputy Secretary of Health and Human Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Deputy_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Deputy Secretary of Health and Human Services").
2. General Counsel of the Department of Health and Human Services
3. Assistant Secretary for Administration
4. [Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assistant_Secretary_for_Planning_and_Evaluation "Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation")
5. Administrator of the [Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Medicare_and_Medicaid_Services "Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services")
6. [Commissioner of Food and Drugs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commissioner_of_Food_and_Drugs "Commissioner of Food and Drugs")
7. Director of the [National Institutes of Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Institutes_of_Health "National Institutes of Health")
8. Assistant Secretary for [Children and Families](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administration_for_Children_and_Families "Administration for Children and Families")
9. Other assistant secretaries (following in the order they took the oath of office)
  1. [Assistant Secretary for Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Assistant_Secretary_for_Health "United States Assistant Secretary for Health")
  2. [Assistant Secretary for Preparedness and Response](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_of_the_Assistant_Secretary_for_Preparedness_and_Response "Office of the Assistant Secretary for Preparedness and Response")
  3. Assistant Secretary for Legislation
  4. Assistant Secretary for Public Affairs
  5. Assistant Secretary for Financial Resources
  6. Assistant Secretary for [Aging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administration_on_Aging "Administration on Aging")
10. Director of the [Centers for Disease Control and Prevention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Disease_Control_and_Prevention "Centers for Disease Control and Prevention")
11. Director, Region 4 ([Atlanta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta "Atlanta"), [Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_(U.S._state) "Georgia (U.S. state)"))

*The Commerce Secretary's office as it looked in the mid-20th century.*

The **United States secretary of commerce** (**SecCom**) is the head of the [United States Department of Commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Commerce "United States Department of Commerce"). The secretary serves as the principal advisor to the [president of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") on all matters relating to [commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commerce "Commerce"). The secretary reports directly to the president and is a statutory member of the [Cabinet of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_United_States "Cabinet of the United States"). The secretary is [appointed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prerogative "Prerogative") by the president, with the [advice and consent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advice_and_Consent_Clause "Advice and Consent Clause") of the [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate"). The secretary of commerce is responsible for promoting American businesses and industries. The department states its mission as 'to foster, promote, and develop the foreign and domestic commerce of the United States'.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Commerce#cite_note-2)

Until 1913, there was one [secretary of commerce and labor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Commerce_and_Labor "United States Department of Commerce and Labor"), uniting this department with the [United States Department of Labor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Labor "United States Department of Labor"), which is now headed by a separate [United States secretary of labor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Labor "United States Secretary of Labor").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Commerce#cite_note-3)

The secretary of commerce is a [Level I position in the Executive Schedule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_Schedule#Level_I "Executive Schedule")[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Commerce#cite_note-4) with an annual salary of [US$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Dollar "US Dollar") 250,600, as of January 2025.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Commerce#cite_note-Salary-5)

The current secretary of commerce is [Howard Lutnick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_Lutnick "Howard Lutnick").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Commerce#cite_note-6)

**Wynn Coggins** is an American business executive and former civil servant. She currently serves as **Chief Growth Officer at [Management Science and Innovation (MSI)](https://www.msiconsulting.com)**. Coggins previously held several senior leadership roles at the United States Department of Commerce, including Acting United States Secretary of Commerce, Acting Deputy Secretary of Commerce, and Acting Chief Financial Officer/Assistant Secretary for Administration.
She served as Acting Secretary of Commerce from January 20, 2021, until March 3, 2021, when Gina Raimondo was sworn in. Coggins then served as Acting Deputy Secretary of Commerce from March 3, 2021, until May 14, 2021, when her successor, Don Graves, was sworn in.
She served as the Acting Chief Financial Officer/Assistant Secretary for Administration from May 2021 until her retirement from Federal service in February, 2022.

## Education

Coggins has a bachelor's degree in civil engineering from [Clemson University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clemson_University "Clemson University") and a Master of Science in information systems technology with a concentration in information resources management from the [George Washington University School of Business](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington_University_School_of_Business "George Washington University School of Business").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wynn_Coggins#cite_note-1)

## Career

### United States Department of Commerce

**Acting Secretary of Commerce**

On January 20, 2021, following the [inauguration of President Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inauguration_of_Joe_Biden "Inauguration of Joe Biden"), Coggins was selected to serve as acting [United States Secretary of Commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Commerce "United States Secretary of Commerce"), pending the confirmation of nominee [Gina Raimondo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gina_Raimondo "Gina Raimondo") by the [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wynn_Coggins#cite_note-2)

**Acting Deputy Secretary of Commerce**

On March 3, 2021, Coggins began to serve as acting [United States Deputy Secretary of Commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Deputy_Secretary_of_Commerce "United States Deputy Secretary of Commerce").

### Deloitte Consulting

**Director of Government Modernization**

Coggins served as a Specialist Executive within the Deloitte Government and Public Services practice starting in February 2022 and became the Director Of Government Modernization in May 2025, serving in that role until December 2025.

### Management Science and Innovation Consulting

**Chief Growth Officer**

On January 7, 2026, Coggins became the [Chief Growth Officer at Management Science and Innovation (MSI)](https://www.msiconsulting.com/wynn-coggins-press-release).

Secretary of Commerce

Wilbur L. Ross, Jr. was sworn in by Vice President Mike Pence as the 39th Secretary of Commerce on February 28, 2017. Secretary Ross is the principal voice of business in the Trump Administration, ensuring that U.S. entrepreneurs and businesses have the tools they need to create jobs and economic opportunity.

Secretary Ross is the former Chairman and Chief Strategy Officer of WL Ross & Co. LLC and has over 55 years of investment banking and private equity experience. He has restructured over $400 billion of assets in the airline, apparel, auto parts, banking, beverage, chemical, credit card, electric utility, food service, furniture, gypsum, homebuilding, insurance, marine transport, mortgage origination and servicing, oil and gas, railcar manufacturing and leasing, real estate, restaurant, shipyard, steel, textile and trucking industries. Secretary Ross has been chairman or lead director of more than 100 companies operating in more than 20 different countries.

Named by Bloomberg Markets as one of the 50 most influential people in global finance, Secretary Ross is the only person elected to both the Private Equity Hall of Fame and the Turnaround Management Hall of Fame. He previously served as privatization adviser to New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani and was appointed by President Bill Clinton to the board of the U.S.-Russia Investment Fund. President Kim Dae-jung awarded Secretary Ross a medal for helping South Korea during its financial crisis and, in November 2014, the Emperor of Japan awarded him the Order of the Rising Sun, Gold and Silver Star.

As a philanthropist, Secretary Ross has served as Chairman of the Japan Society, Trustee of the Brookings Institution and Chairman of its Economic Studies Council, International Counsel Member of the Musée des Arts Décoratifs in Paris, Trustee of the Blenheim Foundation, President of the American Friends of the Rene Magritte Museum in Brussels and Director of the Palm Beach Civic Association. He also was an Advisory Board Member of Yale University School of Management.

Secretary Ross is a graduate of Yale University and Harvard Business School (with distinction). He and his wife Hilary Geary Ross have four children, Jessica Ross, Amanda Ross, Ted Geary and Jack Geary.
